steps.user_message: Here's my situation for 2024 taxes. I'm single, live in Portland OR. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $79,400 (W-2). I also earned $8,900 doing graphic design for 4 clients, got $890 interest from Discover Bank savings and $195 dividends from E*TRADE. I work from home in a 100 sq ft office; rent is $2,050/month, total space 690 sq ft. I paid $2,700 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2018–2019), gave $720 to Northwest Harvest (food bank) I have the receipt, and had $650 in work supplies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Here’s how your 2024 taxes shake out based on what you shared. I’ll cover what’s deductible, whether to itemize, how to handle the home office, and which forms/worksheets to use.

What’s deductible (federal)
- Self-employment (graphic design) expenses on Schedule C:
  - $650 in business supplies (assuming these are for your freelance work; if they’re for your W‑2 job, they’re not deductible federally in 2024).
  - Home office expenses for the freelance business (see “Home office” below).
- Student loan interest: up to $2,500 as an above-the-line deduction, subject to income phase-out. You paid $2,700, but the law caps the deduction at $2,500 and phases it out at higher MAGI. With your income level, expect a partial deduction (you’ll use the Student Loan Interest Deduction Worksheet to compute the allowed amount).
- Half of self-employment tax: deductible above-the-line automatically after you compute SE tax on Schedule SE.
- Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction: generally 20% of your qualified business income from the graphic design activity (computed on Form 8995). This is in addition to the standard deduction and is not an itemized deduction.

Likely not deductible (federal)
- Unreimbursed W-2 employee expenses (including a home office for your W‑2 job and any W‑2 supplies): not deductible for 2024.
- Charitable contributions ($720 to Northwest Harvest) only reduce federal tax if you itemize. See below—standard deduction will likely be better, so this probably won’t reduce your federal tax.

Standard vs itemize (federal)
- Standard deduction for Single in 2024: $14,600.
- Your probable itemized deductions:
  - State and local taxes (SALT) up to $10,000 cap (check your W‑2 Box 17 for state income tax withheld; as a renter you don’t have property tax deductions).
  - Charitable contributions: $720.
  - With no mortgage interest and typical SALT under or near $10,000, your itemized total is likely below $14,600. Conclusion: you’ll likely take the standard deduction.

Home office (for your freelance business)
- Eligibility: space must be used exclusively and regularly for your freelance work, and be your principal place of business for that activity.
- Size: 100 sq ft out of 690 sq ft = about 14.49% business-use percentage.
- You rent at $2,050/month = $24,600/year.
- Two methods:
  - Regular (actual expenses via Form 8829): deduct the business portion of indirect expenses. Based on rent alone, approximate deduction ≈ 14.49% × $24,600 ≈ $3,560. You can also include a business share of renter’s insurance, utilities, and internet (allocated reasonably), if applicable. The deduction can’t create/increase a Schedule C loss; any excess carries forward.
  - Simplified method: $5 per sq ft up to 300 sq ft. For 100 sq ft, that’s $500. Given your rent, the regular method likely gives a much larger deduction.
- Report the home office on Form 8829 (flows to Schedule C) if using the regular method; if using the simplified method, use the simplified worksheet in the Schedule C instructions (no Form 8829).

Rough federal math (to set expectations)
- Schedule C net profit estimate (using regular home office and your $650 supplies):
  - $8,900 income − $650 − ~$3,560 ≈ $4,690 net profit.
- Self-employment tax: about 15.3% of 92.35% of net profit ≈ 15.3% × ~$4,330 ≈ ~$660; half (~$330) is deductible above the line.
- QBI deduction: roughly 20% of qualified business income (after the half-SE-tax adjustment), so on the order of ~$850–$900, subject to final calculations.
- Student loan interest: you paid $2,700; the allowed deduction is up to $2,500 but will be partially phased out at your income—use the worksheet to compute the exact allowable amount.

Where each item goes (federal forms/worksheets)
- Form 1040
  - W‑2 wages from Midwest Health Systems.
  - Taxable interest ($890) and dividends ($195). No Schedule B needed unless either category exceeds $1,500 or you have foreign accounts.
  - Standard deduction (likely).
  - QBI deduction (from Form 8995).
- Schedule C (Form 1040): report $8,900 income; deduct $650 supplies; include home office expense (from Form 8829 if using regular method, or use the simplified method worksheet).
- Form 8829: if using the regular home office method (to compute the business share of rent and other indirect home expenses).
- Schedule SE (Form 1040): compute self-employment tax; half flows to Schedule 1 as an adjustment.
- Schedule 1 (Form 1040):
  - Part I: includes your Schedule C net profit.
  - Part II: includes half of SE tax deduction and the student loan interest deduction.
  - Use the Student Loan Interest Deduction Worksheet (in the Schedule 1 instructions or IRS Pub. 970) to determine the allowable portion.
- Form 8995: Qualified Business Income Deduction.

Oregon notes (brief)
- You’ll file Oregon Form OR‑40 (resident). Oregon starts with your federal AGI, so your Schedule C, home office, and student loan interest deduction flow through. Local Portland/Multnomah/Metro taxes may apply based on your income; check if any local amounts were withheld on your paystub/W‑2.

Documents to gather
- W‑2 from Midwest Health Systems.
- 1099-NEC/1099-K (if any) from clients; if none, you still report the $8,900.
- Records for the $650 supplies.
- Home office details (square footage, rent total, and any utilities/insurance/internet to allocate if using the regular method).
- 1099-INT (Discover Bank) and 1099-DIV (E*TRADE).
- 1098-E (student loan interest) from Cornerstone (you paid >$600 so you should receive one).
- Charitable receipt from Northwest Harvest.

Two quick clarifications to ensure correct treatment
- Were the $650 supplies entirely for your freelance graphic design work? If any portion was for your W‑2 job, that part isn’t deductible federally.
- Is the 100 sq ft office used exclusively for the freelance business (not also for your W‑2 job or personal use)? If it’s mixed with W‑2 work, only the freelance-business use is deductible.

If you confirm those two points, I can firm up the Schedule C/home office numbers and estimate your SE tax, QBI, and the student loan interest deduction more precisely.
